```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
set.seed(258)

plot_cols <- list(
  main        = "#00695c",
  teal        = "#00695c",
  teal_dark   = "#004d40",
  teal_light  = "#e0f2f1",
  blue        = "#c8e6f3",
  blue_soft   = "#eef8fb",
  grey        = "#f5f6f7",
  gray        = "#f5f6f7",
  yellow      = "#fff8e1",
  orange      = "#f9a825",
  text        = "#2f3437",
  muted       = "#667174",
  border      = "#d8dee2",
  code        = "#f3f4f5",
  white       = "#ffffff"
)

plotly_slide_layout <- function(
  p,
  title = NULL,
  x_title = NULL,
  y_title = NULL,
  width = NULL,
  height = 390,
  x_range = NULL,
  y_range = NULL,
  margin = list(l = 70, r = 25, t = 70, b = 60)
) {
  p |>
    layout(
      title = list(
        text = title,
        font = list(size = 16),
        x = 0.02
      ),
      width = width,
      height = height,
      margin = margin,
      xaxis = list(
        title = x_title,
        range = x_range,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      yaxis = list(
        title = y_title,
        range = y_range,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
      plot_bgcolor = "white"
    ) |>
        config(
      displayModeBar = FALSE,
      displaylogo = FALSE,
      scrollZoom = FALSE,
      doubleClick = "reset"
    )
}
```

<script>
document.addEventListener(
  "click",
  function (event) {
    /*
     * Before Quarto removes the Show Solution button,
     * save an exact copy of its HTML.
     */
    const solutionButton = event.target.closest(
      ".btn-exercise-solution"
    );

    if (solutionButton) {
      const buttonGroup = solutionButton.closest(
        ".btn-group-exercise-editor"
      );

      if (buttonGroup) {
        buttonGroup.dataset.solutionButtonHtml =
          solutionButton.outerHTML;
      }

      return;
    }

    /*
     * Detect when the student presses Start Over.
     */
    const startOverButton = event.target.closest(
      '.btn-exercise-editor[aria-label="Start Over"]'
    );

    if (!startOverButton) return;

    const currentSlide = startOverButton.closest("section");

    const buttonGroup = startOverButton.closest(
      ".btn-group-exercise-editor"
    );

    if (!currentSlide || !buttonGroup) return;

    /*
     * Let Quarto perform its normal reset first.
     */
    window.setTimeout(function () {
      const solutions = currentSlide.querySelectorAll(
        ".exercise-solution"
      );

      /*
       * Hide the opened solution.
       */
      solutions.forEach(function (solution) {
        solution.classList.add("d-none");
      });

      /*
       * Restore Show Solution only when it is missing.
       */
      if (
        solutions.length === 0 ||
        buttonGroup.querySelector(".btn-exercise-solution") ||
        !buttonGroup.dataset.solutionButtonHtml
      ) {
        return;
      }

      const holder = document.createElement("div");

      holder.innerHTML =
        buttonGroup.dataset.solutionButtonHtml.trim();

      const restoredButton = holder.firstElementChild;

      if (!restoredButton) return;

      restoredButton.onclick = function () {
        solutions.forEach(function (solution) {
          solution.classList.remove("d-none");
        });

        restoredButton.remove();
      };

      buttonGroup.appendChild(restoredButton);
    }, 0);
  },
  true
);
</script>

<script>
/*
 * Plotly plots inside reveal.js can render at the wrong size (off-centre,
 * too tall) until a resize event fires - which is why they only look right
 * after a manual reload. Force a resize whenever a slide becomes active.
 */
(function () {
  function resizePlots() {
    if (window.Plotly && window.Plotly.Plots) {
      document.querySelectorAll(".js-plotly-plot").forEach(function (gd) {
        try {
          window.Plotly.Plots.resize(gd);
        } catch (e) {}
      });
    } else {
      window.dispatchEvent(new Event("resize"));
    }
  }

  function bind() {
    if (window.Reveal && typeof window.Reveal.on === "function") {
      window.Reveal.on("ready", resizePlots);
      window.Reveal.on("slidechanged", resizePlots);
      window.Reveal.on("slidetransitionend", resizePlots);
    } else {
      window.setTimeout(bind, 200);
    }
  }

  bind();
  window.addEventListener("load", resizePlots);
})();
</script>

## 3.1 Representing Data {#representing-data}

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Data and notation**

Data are **measurements** we write symbolically. For $n$ observations, we use a lowercase letter $x$ with a subscript for the index:

$$x_1, \; x_2, \; \ldots, \; x_n$$

where $x_i$ is one observation and $i = 1, \ldots, n$. The value $n$ is the **sample size**.
:::

<br>

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Condensed form**: $\; x_i : i = 1, \ldots, n$
:::

---

## Tabular Form

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
| Index | 1 | 2 | $\cdots$ | $n$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Observation | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $\cdots$ | $x_n$ |

<br>

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Example.** Five students' study hours:

$$3, \; 4, \; 4, \; 6, \; 8$$

Here $n = 5$, $x_1 = 3$, $x_2 = 4$, $\ldots$, $x_5 = 8$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Why bother with notation?**

Once we write data as $x_1, \ldots, x_n$, every formula in this chapter (mean, variance, IQR) reads the same regardless of what the data actually measure.
:::
:::
::::

## Example: Commute Methods {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-lean}

::: {.col}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>

A survey asked 40 STA258 students how they usually commute to campus.

| Method | Bus | Car | Walk | Train | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 14 | 9 | 5 | 8 | 4 |

**(a)** Is this variable **qualitative** or **quantitative**?

**(b)** Create a **relative frequency** table.

**(c)** Which method is most common?

**(d)** What percentage use **public transport** (Bus and Train)?
:::

:::

::: {.col}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"

commute <- data.frame(
  Method = factor(
    c("Bus", "Car", "Walk", "Train", "Other"),
    levels = c("Bus", "Car", "Walk", "Train", "Other")
  ),
  Frequency = c(14, 9, 5, 8, 4)
)

commute$Percentage <- 100 * commute$Frequency / sum(commute$Frequency)

commute_plot <- plot_ly(
  data = commute,
  x = ~Method,
  y = ~Frequency,
  type = "bar",
  height = 340,
  
  marker = list(
    color = "#00695C",
    line = list(color = "#111111", width = 0.8)
  ),
  
  text = ~Frequency,
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  textfont = list(
    family = "Arial",
    size = 14,
    color = "#111111"
  ),
  
  customdata = ~Percentage,
  hovertemplate = paste0(
    "<b>%{x}</b>",
    "<br>Frequency: %{y}",
    "<br>Percentage: %{customdata:.1f}%",
    "<extra></extra>"
  ),
  
  hoverlabel = list(
    bgcolor = "#111111",
    bordercolor = "#00695C",
    font = list(color = "white", size = 13)
  )
) |>
  layout(
    showlegend = FALSE,
    bargap = 0.34,
    font = list(family = "Arial", color = "#111111"),
    
    xaxis = list(
      title = "",
      showgrid = FALSE,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = "#111111",
      linewidth = 1.4,
      ticks = "outside",
      tickcolor = "#111111",
      ticklen = 5,
      tickfont = list(size = 13, color = "#111111"),
      fixedrange = TRUE
    ),
    
    yaxis = list(
      title = list(text = "Frequency", font = list(size = 13, color = "#111111")),
      range = c(0, 16.5),
      tick0 = 0,
      dtick = 2,
      showgrid = TRUE,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.10)",
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = "#111111",
      linewidth = 1.4,
      ticks = "outside",
      tickcolor = "#111111",
      ticklen = 5,
      tickfont = list(size = 12, color = "#111111"),
      fixedrange = TRUE
    ),
    
    margin = list(l = 70, r = 20, t = 20, b = 55),
    plot_bgcolor = "#FFFFFF",
    paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = FALSE,
    responsive = TRUE
  )

commute_plot
```

## Check in R: Commute Methods

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

freq <- c(Bus = 14, Car = 9, Walk = 5, Train = 8, Other = 4)

freq / sum(freq)                              # relative frequency
names(freq)[which.max(freq)]                  # most common
(freq["Bus"] + freq["Train"]) / sum(freq)     # transit share
```

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

The plot shows daily steps for a sample of students. In the notation $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$, what is $n$?
::::

<div style="
  margin: 7px 0 0 84px;
  font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
  color: #111111;
  line-height: 1.15;
">
  <div style="
    font-size: 24px;
    font-weight: 700;
  ">
    Daily steps data
  </div>

  <div style="
    margin-top: 3px;
    font-size: 16px;
    font-weight: 400;
    color: #333333;
  ">
    Each point represents one observation
  </div>
</div>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"

steps_q <- data.frame(
  student = 1:10,
  steps = c(4, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12)
)

steps_q$observation <- paste0("x", steps_q$student)

steps_plot <- plot_ly(
  data = steps_q,
  x = ~student,
  y = ~steps,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "lines+markers+text",
  height = 220,

  line = list(
    color = "#00695C",
    width = 2
  ),

  marker = list(
    color = "#00695C",
    size = 9,
    line = list(
      color = "#111111",
      width = 0.8
    )
  ),

  text = ~observation,
  textposition = "top center",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,

  textfont = list(
    family = "Arial",
    size = 13,
    color = "#111111"
  ),

  customdata = ~observation,

  hovertemplate = paste0(
    "<b>Observation %{customdata}</b>",
    "<br>Student index: %{x}",
    "<br>Daily steps: %{y} thousand",
    "<extra></extra>"
  ),

  hoverlabel = list(
    bgcolor = "#111111",
    bordercolor = "#00695C",
    font = list(
      family = "Arial",
      size = 13,
      color = "#FFFFFF"
    )
  )
) |>
  layout(
    showlegend = FALSE,
    hovermode = "closest",

    font = list(
      family = "Arial",
      color = "#111111"
    ),

    xaxis = list(
      title = list(
        text = "Student index",
        standoff = 8,
        font = list(
          size = 13,
          color = "#111111"
        )
      ),

      range = c(0.55, 10.45),

      tickmode = "array",
      tickvals = 1:10,
      ticktext = as.character(1:10),

      showgrid = FALSE,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,

      linecolor = "#111111",
      linewidth = 1.3,

      ticks = "outside",
      tickcolor = "#111111",
      ticklen = 4,

      tickfont = list(
        size = 12,
        color = "#111111"
      ),

      automargin = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE
    ),

    yaxis = list(
      title = list(
        text = "Steps (thousands)",
        standoff = 8,
        font = list(
          size = 13,
          color = "#111111"
        )
      ),

      range = c(2.2, 13.8),
      tick0 = 2.5,
      dtick = 2.5,

      showgrid = TRUE,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.10)",
      gridwidth = 1,

      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,

      linecolor = "#111111",
      linewidth = 1.3,

      ticks = "outside",
      tickcolor = "#111111",
      ticklen = 4,

      tickfont = list(
        size = 12,
        color = "#111111"
      ),

      automargin = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE
    ),

    margin = list(
      l = 82,
      r = 24,
      t = 12,
      b = 48
    ),

    plot_bgcolor = "#FFFFFF",
    paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
```

## 3.2 Numerical Measures {#numerical-measures}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Centre</span>
Where is the "typical" value? Mean, median, mode.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Spread</span>
How dispersed are the values? Variance, SD, range, IQR.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Position</span>
Where does one value sit relative to the rest? Percentiles, quartiles.
:::
::::

<br>

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
No single number tells the whole story. We pair centre with spread, and read both alongside a plot.
:::

---

## 3.2.1 Mean

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**Sample mean** $\bar{x}$

For a sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$,

$$\bar{x} \; = \; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i}{n} \; = \; \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n}{n}$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
The mean is the **arithmetic average** - the one most people mean when they say "average."
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

hours <- c(3, 4, 4, 6, 8)

sum(hours)        # numerator
length(hours)     # n
mean(hours)       # built-in
```
:::
::::

---

## 3.2.2 Median

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Median**

The middle value of a data set once the observations are sorted in ascending order.

Let $x_{(1)}, x_{(2)}, \ldots, x_{(n)}$ be the sorted values. Then:

- If $n$ is **odd**:  $\;\;$ Median $=$ observation $\left(\dfrac{n+1}{2}\right)$
- If $n$ is **even**:  $\;\;$ Median $=$ average of observations $\left(\dfrac{n}{2}\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{n}{2} + 1\right)$
:::

---

## Median in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

odd_data  <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5)
even_data <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9)

sort(odd_data)         # see the order
median(odd_data)       # middle value

sort(even_data)
median(even_data)      # average of the two middle values
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Sorted odd:** 1, 1, **3**, 4, 5 → middle value is 3.

**Sorted even:** 1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 9 → middle pair is **3** and **4**, so median $= (3 + 4)/2 = 3.5$.
:::
:::
::::

---

## 3.2.3 Mode

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**Mode**

The most frequently occurring value in a data set.

A data set can have one mode (**unimodal**), two modes (**bimodal**), more than two modes (**multimodal**), or no mode if every value occurs equally often.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 8)

# R has no built-in mode() for the statistical mode
counts <- table(x)
counts                            # frequency of each value
names(counts)[which.max(counts)]  # the mode
```
:::
::::

---

## 3.2.4 Variance

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Sample variance** $s^2$

A measure of spread based on the squared deviations from the sample mean:

$$s^{2} \; = \; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}$$

where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Each term is squared**, so $s^2 \ge 0$ always.

The **units** of $s^2$ are the units of the data **squared** (e.g. dollars²). That is awkward to interpret, which is why we usually report the standard deviation instead.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Why divide by $n-1$?

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Bessel's correction.** We use sample data $\bar{x}$ to estimate the (unknown) population mean $\mu$. That estimation step "uses up" one piece of information.

Dividing by $n - 1$ instead of $n$ corrects for this, and makes $s^2$ an **unbiased** estimator of the population variance.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
You will see a formal proof of this in **STA260**. For now, just remember:

- **Sample** variance → divide by $n - 1$
- **Population** variance → divide by $N$
:::

---

## Variance in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(2, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8)

# Step by step
xbar <- mean(x)
xbar

dev  <- x - xbar          # deviations
sq   <- dev^2             # squared deviations
sum(sq) / (length(x) - 1) # variance by formula

var(x)                    # built-in (same answer)
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Tip.** Build the table $(x_i, x_i - \bar{x}, (x_i - \bar{x})^2)$ on paper before reaching for `var()`. Several exam questions ask for the table.
:::
:::
::::

---

## 3.2.5 Standard Deviation

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**Sample standard deviation** $s$

$$s \; = \; \sqrt{s^{2}}$$

where $s^2$ is the sample variance.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
Taking the square root returns us to the **original units**, which is why we usually report $s$ rather than $s^2$ in practice.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(2, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8)

var(x)        # variance
sd(x)         # standard deviation
sqrt(var(x))  # the same thing
```
:::
::::

---

## 3.2.6 Range

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**Range**

$$\text{Range} \; = \; \max(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \; - \; \min(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$$

The difference between the largest and smallest observations.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
**Caution.** The range uses only two values, so a single extreme observation can change it dramatically. It is a quick summary, not a robust one.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 30)

min(x)
max(x)
max(x) - min(x)   # range

range(x)          # returns min and max as a vector
diff(range(x))    # also gives the range
```
:::
::::

---

## 3.2.7 Percentiles

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**$p^{\text{th}}$ percentile**

In an ordered data set, the $p^{\text{th}}$ percentile is a value at or below which approximately $p\%$ of the observations fall.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Example.** A class writes a difficult test and a student scores 72%. Although 72% is a B-, the test was hard. In fact, this mark sits at the **90th percentile** for this test - approximately 90% of the class scored at or below 72%.

A relative position can matter more than the raw mark.
:::

---

## 3.2.8 Quartiles

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Quartiles**

Three values that split the sorted data into four equal-size groups.

- **First quartile** $Q_1$: 25% of values below it.
- **Second quartile** $Q_2$: 50% of values below it. **This is the median.**
- **Third quartile** $Q_3$: 75% of values below it.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
Quartiles are just three specific percentiles: $Q_1 = P_{25}$, $Q_2 = P_{50}$, $Q_3 = P_{75}$.
:::

---

## Interquartile Range (IQR)

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**IQR**

$$\text{IQR} \; = \; Q_3 - Q_1$$

The width of the middle 50% of the data.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
Unlike the range, the IQR is **resistant to outliers** because it depends on $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ rather than directly using the minimum and maximum.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 30)

summary(x)        # min, Q1, median, mean, Q3, max
quantile(x)       # the five-number quartile breaks
IQR(x)            # Q3 - Q1
```
:::
::::

---

## Example: Final Exam Scores {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-lean}

::: {.col}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>

The final exam scores for $12$ students are:

$$52, 58, 61, 65, 70, 72, 75, 78, 82, 86, 90, 96$$

**(a)** Find the **median**.

**(b)** Find the **first quartile**, $Q_{1}$.

**(c)** Find the **third quartile**, $Q_{3}$.

**(d)** Find the **interquartile range** (IQR).

**(e)** Using the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule, which scores would be flagged as unusually low or high?
:::

:::

::: {.col}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

exam <- data.frame(
  score = c(52, 58, 61, 65, 70, 72, 75, 78, 82, 86, 90, 96)
)

exam$q1 <- unname(quantile(exam$score, 0.25))
exam$median <- median(exam$score)
exam$q3 <- unname(quantile(exam$score, 0.75))
exam$iqr <- exam$q3 - exam$q1

lower_fence <- exam$q1[1] - 1.5 * exam$iqr[1]
upper_fence <- exam$q3[1] + 1.5 * exam$iqr[1]

whisker_low <- min(
  exam$score[exam$score >= lower_fence]
)

whisker_high <- max(
  exam$score[exam$score <= upper_fence]
)

q1_value <- exam$q1[1]
median_value <- exam$median[1]
q3_value <- exam$q3[1]

exam$point_y <- c(
  1.00, 0.95, 1.05, 0.97,
  1.04, 0.94, 1.06, 0.96,
  1.03, 0.95, 1.05, 1.00
)

exam_plot <- plot_ly(
  data = exam,
  x = ~score,
  y = ~point_y,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers",
  height = 245,

  marker = list(
    color = "#00695C",
    size = 10,
    line = list(
      color = "#111111",
      width = 0.9
    )
  ),

  hovertemplate = paste0(
    "<b>Final exam score: %{x}</b>",
    "<extra></extra>"
  ),

  hoverlabel = list(
    bgcolor = "#111111",
    bordercolor = "#00695C",
    font = list(
      family = "Arial",
      size = 13,
      color = "#FFFFFF"
    )
  )
) |>
  layout(
    showlegend = FALSE,
    hovermode = "closest",
    dragmode = FALSE,

    font = list(
      family = "Arial",
      color = "#111111"
    ),

    shapes = list(
      list(
        type = "line",
        x0 = whisker_low,
        x1 = whisker_high,
        y0 = 1,
        y1 = 1,
        layer = "below",
        line = list(
          color = "#111111",
          width = 2
        )
      ),

      list(
        type = "rect",
        x0 = q1_value,
        x1 = q3_value,
        y0 = 0.87,
        y1 = 1.13,
        layer = "below",
        fillcolor = "rgba(0,105,92,0.18)",
        line = list(
          color = "#00695C",
          width = 2.2
        )
      ),

      list(
        type = "line",
        x0 = median_value,
        x1 = median_value,
        y0 = 0.87,
        y1 = 1.13,
        layer = "below",
        line = list(
          color = "#111111",
          width = 3
        )
      ),

      list(
        type = "line",
        x0 = whisker_low,
        x1 = whisker_low,
        y0 = 0.94,
        y1 = 1.06,
        layer = "below",
        line = list(
          color = "#111111",
          width = 2
        )
      ),

      list(
        type = "line",
        x0 = whisker_high,
        x1 = whisker_high,
        y0 = 0.94,
        y1 = 1.06,
        layer = "below",
        line = list(
          color = "#111111",
          width = 2
        )
      )
    ),

    xaxis = list(
      title = list(
        text = "Final exam score",
        standoff = 8,

        )
      ),
```

## 3.3 Graphical Techniques {#graphical-techniques}

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Why plot at all?</span>
Numbers alone hide the **shape** of a distribution. A picture reveals skewness, gaps, clusters, and unusual values.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Two workhorses</span>
**Histograms** show the full shape of one variable. **Boxplots** highlight centre, spread, and outliers, and stack neatly for group comparisons.
:::
::::

<br>

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Pair numbers with pictures.** A mean of 65 looks different on a symmetric bell than on a right-skewed pile with a long tail. Always look at both.
:::

---

## Skewness

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Skewness**

A measure of the **symmetry** (or lack of it) in the distribution of data.
:::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Left-skewed</span>
Long tail on the **left**. Most values bunched on the right. Also called **negatively skewed**.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Symmetric</span>
Roughly mirror-image around the centre. Mean $\approx$ median.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Right-skewed</span>
Long tail on the **right**. Most values bunched on the left. Also called **positively skewed**.
:::
::::

---

## Skewness Illustrated {.compact}

```{r}

#| results: asis
```

::: {.thinkbox}
The **tail** points in the direction of the skew. “Right-skewed” means the tail extends to the right. The mean is pulled toward the tail, while the median remains closer to the bulk of the data.
:::

---

## Skewness vs Mean & Median

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Rule of thumb**

- Left-skewed: **Mean $<$ Median**
- Symmetric: **Mean $\approx$ Median**
- Right-skewed: **Mean $>$ Median**

The mean is pulled toward the long tail. The median is not.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# Right-skewed sample (waiting times)
set.seed(258)
wait <- rexp(200, rate = 0.1)

mean(wait)
median(wait)
# mean > median  ->  right-skewed
```
:::
::::

---

## Outliers

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Outlier**

A data point that appears to lie outside the overall pattern of the rest of the data.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Do not just delete outliers.**

Investigate first - is it a data-entry error, a measurement error, or a genuine rare observation? The right call depends on the cause.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Common causes**

- Transcription error (typing 100 instead of 10)
- Measurement error (broken instrument)
- A real but unusual case (a millionaire in a sample of incomes)
:::
:::
::::

---

## 3.3.1 Histograms

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Histogram**

A plot of a **quantitative** variable, built by:

1. Splitting the range of the data into intervals (**bins**).
2. Counting how many observations fall in each bin.
3. Drawing a bar over each bin with height equal to its frequency.

The $x$-axis shows the bins, and the $y$-axis shows frequency (or relative frequency).
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Frequency vs relative frequency.** Frequency histograms show raw counts; relative-frequency histograms show proportions (each bar height $= f_i / F$, where $F = \sum f_i$).
:::

---

## Histogram Construction {.compact}

::: {.examplebox}
**Table 3.1 - How a histogram is constructed**
:::

| Class Interval | Frequency | Relative Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| $[a_1, b_1)$ | $f_1$ | $r_1 = f_1 / F$ |
| $[a_2, b_2)$ | $f_2$ | $r_2 = f_2 / F$ |
| $[a_3, b_3)$ | $f_3$ | $r_3 = f_3 / F$ |
| $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ |
| $[a_m, b_m]$ | $f_m$ | $r_m = f_m / F$ |
| **Total** | $F = \sum_{i=1}^{m} f_i$ | $1$ |

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**The histograms in this chapter use equal-width bins.** We choose a width that shows the structure of the data without too much noise.
:::

---

## Histogram in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# Old Faithful eruption waiting times
data(faithful)

waiting <- faithful$waiting

hist(waiting,
     main = "Old Faithful waiting times",
     xlab = "Waiting time (minutes)",
     col  = "#00695c",
     border = "white")
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Try it.** Add the argument `breaks = 5` (or 30) to the `hist()` call to see how bin width changes the picture.

The faithful waiting times are **bimodal** - two distinct clusters around 55 and 80 minutes.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Bin Width Matters {.compact}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-height: 3.2

data(faithful)

waiting_times <- faithful$waiting
waiting_range <- range(waiting_times)

make_bin_plot <- function(number_of_bins, panel_label) {

  bin_size <- diff(waiting_range) / number_of_bins

  plot_ly(
    x = waiting_times,
    type = "histogram",

    xbins = list(
      start = waiting_range[1],
      end = waiting_range[2] + 0.001,
      size = bin_size
    ),

    marker = list(
      color = "#00695C",
      line = list(
        color = "#FFFFFF",
        width = 0.8
      )
    ),

    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>", panel_label, "</b>",
      "<br>Bin position: %{x:.1f} minutes",
      "<br>Frequency: %{y}",
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),

    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
    layout(
      bargap = 0.03,

      xaxis = list(
        range = c(42, 100),

        showgrid = FALSE,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,

        linecolor = "#111111",
        linewidth = 1.3,

        ticks = "outside",
        tickcolor = "#111111",
        ticklen = 4,

        tickfont = list(
          family = "Arial",
          size = 11,
          color = "#111111"
        ),

        fixedrange = TRUE
      ),

      yaxis = list(
        showgrid = TRUE,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.09)",
        gridwidth = 1,

        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,

        linecolor = "#111111",
        linewidth = 1.3,

        ticks = "outside",
        tickcolor = "#111111",
        ticklen = 4,

        tickfont = list(
          family = "Arial",
          size = 11,
          color = "#111111"
        ),

        fixedrange = TRUE
      ),

      plot_bgcolor = "#FFFFFF",
      paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"
    )
}

plot_5_bins <- make_bin_plot(
  number_of_bins = 5,

)
```

## 3.3.2 Boxplots

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Boxplot** (box-and-whisker plot)

A five-number summary in graphical form:

- **Box** spans from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$.
- **Line** inside the box marks the median.
- **Whiskers** extend out to the most extreme observation **inside** the outlier cutoffs.
- **Dots** beyond the whiskers are flagged as potential outliers.
:::

---

## The $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ Rule

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Outlier cutoffs (fences)**

$$\text{Lower cutoff} = Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$$
$$\text{Upper cutoff} = Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$$

Any value outside these cutoffs is flagged as a **potential outlier**.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Example.** A dataset has $Q_1 = 5$, $Q_3 = 11$, so $\text{IQR} = 6$ and $1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 9$.

- Lower cutoff: $5 - 9 = -4$
- Upper cutoff: $11 + 9 = 20$

Any value below $-4$ or above $20$ would be flagged.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Boxplot in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 30)

# Five-number summary
summary(x)

boxplot(x,
        horizontal = TRUE,
        main = "Bus wait times (minutes)",
        col  = "#00695c")
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**What to look for**

- Where does the median sit inside the box? Off-centre suggests skew.
- How long are the whiskers? Unequal whisker lengths also suggest skew.
- Any dots? Those are potential outliers.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Skewness from a Boxplot

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

set.seed(3)

left_box_values <- 30 - rgamma(
  150,
  shape = 3,
  rate = 0.5
)

symmetric_box_values <- rnorm(
  150,
  mean = 10,
  sd = 3
)

right_box_values <- rgamma(
  150,
  shape = 3,
  rate = 0.5
)

box_skew_plot <- plot_ly(
  height = 300
) |>
  add_trace(
    x = left_box_values,
    y = rep(
      "Left-skewed",
      length(left_box_values)
    ),

    type = "box",
    orientation = "h",
    name = "Left-skewed",

    boxpoints = "outliers",
    fillcolor = "#9C8CD4",

    line = list(
      color = "#111111",
      width = 1.5
    ),

    marker = list(
      color = "#B32025",
      size = 7,
      line = list(
        color = "#111111",
        width = 0.8
      )
    ),

    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Left-skewed distribution</b>",
      "<br>Value: %{x:.1f}",
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),

    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    x = symmetric_box_values,
    y = rep(
      "Symmetric",
      length(symmetric_box_values)
    ),

    type = "box",
    orientation = "h",
    name = "Symmetric",

    boxpoints = "outliers",
    fillcolor = "#00AA88",

    line = list(
      color = "#111111",
      width = 1.5
    ),

    marker = list(
      color = "#B32025",
      size = 7,
      line = list(
        color = "#111111",
        width = 0.8
      )
    ),

    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Symmetric distribution</b>",
      "<br>Value: %{x:.1f}",
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),

    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    x = right_box_values,
    y = rep(
      "Right-skewed",
      length(right_box_values)
    ),

    type = "box",
    orientation = "h",
    name = "Right-skewed",

    boxpoints = "outliers",
    fillcolor = "#F9A825",

    line = list(
      color = "#111111",
      width = 1.5
    ),

    marker = list(
      color = "#B32025",
      size = 7,
      line = list(
        color = "#111111",
        width = 0.8
      )
    ),

    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Right-skewed distribution</b>",
      "<br>Value: %{x:.1f}",
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),

    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  layout(
    showlegend = FALSE,
    hovermode = "closest",
    dragmode = FALSE,
    boxgap = 0.38,

    font = list(
      family = "Arial",
      color = "#111111"
    ),

    xaxis = list(
      title = list(
        text = "Value",
        standoff = 10,
        font = list(
          family = "Arial",
          size = 14,
          color = "#111111"
        )
      ),

      showgrid = TRUE,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.09)",
      gridwidth = 1,

      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,

      linecolor = "#111111",
      linewidth = 1.4,

      ticks = "outside",
      tickcolor = "#111111",
      ticklen = 5,

      tickfont = list(
        family = "Arial",
        size = 12,
        color = "#111111"
      ),

      automargin = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE
    ),

    yaxis = list(
      categoryorder = "array",
      categoryarray = c(
        "Right-skewed",
        "Symmetric",
        "Left-skewed"
      ),

      showgrid = FALSE,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = "#111111",
      linewidth = 1.4,

      tickfont = list(
        family = "Arial",
        size = 14,
        color = "#111111"
      ),

      automargin = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE
    ),

    hoverlabel = list(
      bgcolor = "#111111",
      bordercolor = "#B32025",

      font = list(
        family = "Arial",
        size = 13,
        color = "#FFFFFF"
      )
    ),

    margin = list(
      l = 130,
      r = 34,
      t = 16,
      b = 55
    ),

    plot_bgcolor = "#FFFFFF",
    paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = FALSE,
    responsive = TRUE
  )

htmltools::div(
  style = paste0(
    "width: 92%;",
    "margin: 4px auto 0 auto;"
  ),
  box_skew_plot
)
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Reading skew from a box.** Median **closer to $Q_3$** with a long lower whisker suggests left skew. Median **closer to $Q_1$** with a long upper whisker suggests right skew. The longer tail points in the direction of the skew.
:::

## Example: Online Quiz Times {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-lean}

::: {.col}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>

A professor records the time, in minutes, that students spent completing an online quiz:

$$12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 35, 50$$

**(a)** Would a **histogram** or **boxplot** better show the **shape** of the distribution?

**(b)** Would a **boxplot** or **histogram** be better for **identifying possible outliers**?

**(c)** Describe the likely **shape**: symmetric, left-skewed, or right-skewed.

**(d)** Which value seems most likely to be an outlier?
:::

:::

::: {.col}

```{r}

tickmode = "array",
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

set.seed(258)

restaurant_a <- data.frame(
  Restaurant = "Restaurant A",
  Time = rnorm(
    80,
    mean = 31,
    sd = 2.1
  )
)

restaurant_b <- data.frame(
  Restaurant = "Restaurant B",
  Time = c(
    rnorm(
      76,
      mean = 32,
      sd = 5.8
    ),
    55,
    61,
    72,
    80
  )
)

restaurant_plot <- plot_ly(
  height = 230
) |>
  add_trace(
    data = restaurant_a,
    x = ~Time,
    y = ~Restaurant,
    type = "box",
    orientation = "h",
    name = "Restaurant A",

    boxpoints = "outliers",

    fillcolor = "rgba(0,105,92,0.24)",

    line = list(
      color = "#00695C",
      width = 2.2
    ),

    marker = list(
      color = "#00695C",
      size = 7,
      line = list(
        color = "#111111",
        width = 0.6
```

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

Look at the boxplot. What kind of skewness does this shape suggest?
::::

<div style="
  width: 90%;
  margin: 6px auto 0 auto;
  font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
  color: #111111;
  line-height: 1.15;
">
  <span style="
    display: block;
    font-size: 24px !important;
    font-weight: 700 !important;
    line-height: 1.15;
    color: #111111;
  ">
    Reading skewness from a boxplot
  </span>

  <span style="
    display: block;
    margin-top: 4px;
    font-size: 16px !important;
    font-weight: 400 !important;
    line-height: 1.2;
    color: #444444 !important;
  ">
    Compare the median position and whisker lengths
  </span>
</div>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"

set.seed(258)

left_skew_q <- data.frame(
  value = 30 - rgamma(
    160,
    shape = 3,
    rate = 0.5
  )
)

box_summary <- boxplot.stats(
  left_skew_q$value,
  coef = 1.5
)

lower_whisker <- box_summary$stats[1]
q1_value <- box_summary$stats[2]
median_value <- box_summary$stats[3]
q3_value <- box_summary$stats[4]
upper_whisker <- box_summary$stats[5]
outlier_values <- box_summary$out

hover_values <- data.frame(
  value = c(
    lower_whisker,
    q1_value,
    median_value,
    q3_value,
    upper_whisker
  ),
  position = rep(1, 5)
)

value_range <- range(
  left_skew_q$value,
  finite = TRUE
)

axis_padding <- diff(value_range) * 0.08

skew_boxplot <- plot_ly(
  height = 190
) |>
  add_markers(
    data = hover_values,
    x = ~value,
    y = ~position,

    marker = list(
      color = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
      size = 18
    ),

    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Boxplot value</b>",
      "<br>Value: %{x:.1f}",
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),

    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_markers(
    x = outlier_values,
    y = rep(
      1,
      length(outlier_values)
    ),

    marker = list(
      color = "#B32025",
      size = 8,
      line = list(
        color = "#111111",
        width = 0.8
      )
    ),

    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Potential outlier</b>",
      "<br>Value: %{x:.1f}",
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),

    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  layout(
    showlegend = FALSE,
    hovermode = "closest",
    dragmode = FALSE,

    font = list(
      family = "Arial",
      color = "#111111"
    ),

    shapes = list(
      # Lower whisker
      list(
        type = "line",
        xref = "x",
        yref = "y",

        x0 = lower_whisker,
        x1 = q1_value,
        y0 = 1,
        y1 = 1,

        line = list(
          color = "#004D40",
          width = 3
        )
      ),

      # Upper whisker
      list(
        type = "line",
        xref = "x",
        yref = "y",

        x0 = q3_value,
        x1 = upper_whisker,
        y0 = 1,
        y1 = 1,

        line = list(
          color = "#004D40",
          width = 3
        )
      ),

      # Lower whisker cap
      list(
        type = "line",
        xref = "x",
        yref = "y",

        x0 = lower_whisker,
        x1 = lower_whisker,
        y0 = 0.86,
        y1 = 1.14,

        line = list(
          color = "#004D40",
          width = 3
        )
      ),

      # Upper whisker cap
      list(
        type = "line",
        xref = "x",
        yref = "y",

        x0 = upper_whisker,
        x1 = upper_whisker,
        y0 = 0.86,
        y1 = 1.14,

        line = list(
          color = "#004D40",
          width = 3
        )
      ),

      # Interquartile-range box
      list(
        type = "rect",
        xref = "x",
        yref = "y",

        x0 = q1_value,
        x1 = q3_value,
        y0 = 0.72,
        y1 = 1.28,

        fillcolor = "rgba(0,105,92,0.32)",

        line = list(
          color = "#004D40",
          width = 3
        )
      ),

      # Median
      list(
        type = "line",
        xref = "x",
        yref = "y",

        x0 = median_value,
        x1 = median_value,
        y0 = 0.72,
        y1 = 1.28,

        line = list(
          color = "#111111",
          width = 3
        )
      )
    ),

    xaxis = list(
      title = list(
        text = "Value",
        standoff = 9,

        font = list(
          family = "Arial",
          size = 14,
          color = "#111111"
        )
      ),

      range = c(
        value_range[1] - axis_padding,
        value_range[2] + axis_padding
      ),

      showgrid = TRUE,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.09)",
      gridwidth = 1,

      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,

      linecolor = "#111111",
      linewidth = 1.4,

      ticks = "outside",
      tickcolor = "#111111",
      ticklen = 5,

      tickfont = list(
        family = "Arial",
        size = 12,
        color = "#111111"
      ),

      automargin = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE
    ),

    yaxis = list(
      title = "",
      range = c(0.45, 1.55),

      showticklabels = FALSE,
      showgrid = FALSE,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = "#111111",
      linewidth = 1.4,

      fixedrange = TRUE
    ),

    hoverlabel = list(
      bgcolor = "#111111",
      bordercolor = "#00695C",

      font = list(
        family = "Arial",
        size = 13,
        color = "#FFFFFF"
      )
    ),

    margin = list(
      l = 28,
      r = 28,
      t = 8,
      b = 48
    ),

    plot_bgcolor = "#FFFFFF",
    paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = FALSE,
    responsive = TRUE
  )

htmltools::div(
  style = paste0(
    "width: 90%;",
    "margin: 1px auto 0 auto;"
  ),
  skew_boxplot
)
```

- The distribution is right-skewed
- [The distribution is left-skewed]{.correct data-explanation="The lower whisker and lower tail extend farther to the left. The longer tail points in the direction of the skew, so the distribution is left-skewed."}
- The distribution is symmetric
- There must be a high outlier

## Comparing Two Groups

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

groupA <- c(14, 15, 14, 16, 15, 14, 16, 15, 15, 16)
groupB <- c( 8, 12, 15, 19, 18, 11, 17, 20, 20, 10)

mean(groupA); sd(groupA)
mean(groupB); sd(groupB)

boxplot(list(A = groupA, B = groupB),
        col = c("#00695c", "#f9a825"),
        main = "Quiz scores by group")
```

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Same mean, different stories.**

Both groups have $\bar{x} = 15$, but Group B is much more spread out. Mean alone hides this - the standard deviation and the side-by-side boxplots make it obvious.

## Worked Example: Variance Table {.compact}

::: {.examplebox}
**Six study hours**: $x = 2, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8$. $\;\;\bar{x} = 30 / 6 = 5$.
:::

| $x_i$ | $x_i - \bar{x}$ | $(x_i - \bar{x})^2$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | $2 - 5 = -3$ | $(-3)^2 = 9$ |
| 4 | $4 - 5 = -1$ | $(-1)^2 = 1$ |
| 4 | $4 - 5 = -1$ | $(-1)^2 = 1$ |
| 6 | $6 - 5 = +1$ | $(+1)^2 = 1$ |
| 6 | $6 - 5 = +1$ | $(+1)^2 = 1$ |
| 8 | $8 - 5 = +3$ | $(+3)^2 = 9$ |
| **Sum** | $0$ | $22$ |

$$s^2 = \frac{22}{6 - 1} = 4.4, \quad s = \sqrt{4.4} \approx 2.10$$

## Chapter Summary {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Centre</span>
**Mean** uses every value.<br>**Median** is resistant to extremes.<br>**Mode** is the most common value.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Spread</span>
**Range** = max − min (sensitive).<br>**IQR** = $Q_3 - Q_1$ (resistant).<br>**SD** $s$ is the typical distance from $\bar{x}$.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Shape</span>
Read **skewness** from a histogram (which way does the tail point?) or a boxplot (which whisker is longer?).
:::
::::

<br>

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One slide takeaway.** Always report a number **and** a picture. A mean without a histogram, or a histogram without a summary, leaves half the story untold.
:::
